Please answer this question with a number--which of the following best apply to the design in the study: 
        (1) totally fun first (i.e., Entertainment game reappropriated), 
        (2) mostly fun first (i.e., design workshop with disabled stakeholders),
        (3) both fun and utility first (i.e., design workshop with diverse stakeholders), 
        (4) mostly utility first (i.e., primary utilitarian mechanic designed first),
        (5) totally utility first (i.e., made by clinicians or specialists, fun incorporated later)
reasoning: The system is described as a computer game specifically designed to help children practice ASL skills and encourage linguistic development, with strong emphasis on educational goals, language development, and ASL recognition. Vocabulary and phrases were selected with educational technology specialists and linguists to match classroom instruction and developmental goals, indicating a primary utilitarian (educational/clinical) purpose with game elements layered on, rather than an entertainment game repurposed or a co-designed fun-first process.

Please answer this question with a number--which of the following best apply to the design in the study: 
        (1) entirely solo (i.e., solitaire),
        (2) mostly solo (i.e., playing against AI in single-player StarCraft),
        (3) mix of solo and social affordances (i.e., animal crossing),
        (4) mostly social, but aspects are independent (i.e., house on hill haunt transition),
        (5) entirely social (i.e., tag)
reasoning: The CopyCat ASL game is described as an educational computer game where an individual child plays at a workstation, interacting with tutorial videos, a live camera feed, and an animated character, and issuing commands via ASL to control the character. All descriptions of gameplay, data collection, and system configuration involve a single child at a time with no mention of multiple players, peers, or social interaction within the game. Thus the design is entirely solo.

question:
Please answer this question with a number--which of the following best apply to the design in the study: 
        (1) entirely turn-based (i.e., tic tac toe),
        (2) follows a set of steps (i.e., viticulture's dynamic turn ordering),
        (3) turns are taken, but some actions can be taken at any time (i.e., pandemic),
        (4) most actions can be taken at any time, but there are some phases (i.e., PvP death reset timer),
        (5) entirely simultaneous (i.e., race)
reasoning: Gameplay is structured as the child repeatedly performs discrete sign-phrase tasks: click to wake the character, sign the phrase, click to end the interaction. This defines clear, ordered turns/phases for each action with no indication of overlapping or real-time simultaneous actions, fitting an entirely turn-based structure.

question:
Please answer this question with a number--which of the following best apply to the design in the study: 
        (1) entirely synchronous (i.e., real time strategy game),
        (2) mostly synchronous with a few asynchronous affordances (i.e., league of legends),
        (3) equal mix of synchronous and asynchronous affordances (i.e., helldivers 2),
        (4) mostly asynchronous with few synchronous affordances (i.e. cookie clicker),
        (5) entirely asynchronous (i.e., chess by postage mail)
reasoning: The game involves real-time interaction: the child clicks to wake the character, signs a phrase, and clicks to end the interaction, with the system (or Wizard) evaluating the sign during game play. There is no mention of turn-based delays or offline/asynchronous play; all described interactions occur in real time within a continuous play session, fitting an entirely synchronous design.

        (1) entirely competitive (i.e., spit card game),
        (2) mostly competitive, but sometimes collaboration is important (i.e., forbidden island),
        (3) mix of competitive and collaborative (i.e., mario party 2 vs 2 mini-games),
        (4) mostly collaborative (i.e., animal crossing),
        (5) entirely collaborative (i.e., pandemic)
reasoning: The CopyCat game is described as an educational tool for individual children to practice ASL phrases with a computer character, with no mention of players competing or cooperating with each other. The interaction is between a single child and the system to help language development, indicating an entirely collaborative design focused on helping the player succeed rather than competition.

question:
Please answer this question with a number--which of the following best apply to the design in the study: 
        (1) entirely symmetrical (i.e., tic tac toe),
        (2) mostly symmetrical (i.e., undertale's differing NPC behaviors based on previous playthroughs),
        (3) both symmetrical and asymmetrical (i.e., pandemic with its similar turn structure but different character abilities),
        (4) mostly asymmetrical (i.e., tag),
        (5) entirely asymmetrical (i.e., keep talking, nobody explodes)
reasoning: The game is a single-player educational ASL practice system where the child signs phrases to control an on-screen character (Iris) and interact with game elements. There are no opposing or cooperating player roles with shared rules; instead, the child is the only active player and the system acts as a non-human evaluator/partner. This makes the interaction structure fully asymmetric between human and system, best matching an entirely asymmetrical design.
